# Bosnian Serb war crimes suspect Radovan Karadzic arrested in Serbia

**BELGRADE, Serbia (CNN) —** Radovan Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb leader accused of genocide and crimes against humanity during the 1992-95 Bosnian war, has been arrested after more than a decade on the run, Serbian officials said Monday.

Karadzic was taken into custody by Serbian security forces and brought before an investigative judge in Belgrade, according to Serbia’s presidency and the country’s war crimes prosecutor’s office. Officials said he had been living under a false identity and working as a practitioner of alternative medicine.

He is expected to be transferred to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague, Netherlands, where he faces charges including genocide, persecution, extermination, murder and deportation. Karadzic has denied wrongdoing and is presumed innocent unless convicted.

The tribunal accuses Karadzic of helping orchestrate the siege of Sarajevo, in which thousands of civilians were killed, and the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica, where Bosnian Serb forces killed about 8,000 Muslim men and boys.

Former U.S. diplomat Richard Holbrooke, who brokered the Dayton peace agreement that ended the war, called Karadzic one of the principal architects of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia. Holbrooke compared the fugitive’s significance to that of Osama bin Laden and said the arrest offered a chance for justice for the victims of the conflict.

Holbrooke also rejected claims that he had promised Karadzic immunity from prosecution in exchange for withdrawing from public life.

British Foreign Secretary David Miliband welcomed the arrest, calling it an important moment for international justice and for Serbia’s relationship with Europe.

“This is very good news,” Miliband said, praising the Serbian authorities and stressing that those accused of the gravest crimes must be held accountable.

Paddy Ashdown, the former international high representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina, described the arrest as a major breakthrough. He said Karadzic’s trial could become one of the most significant war crimes proceedings since Nuremberg and would allow survivors to hear the evidence tested in court.

European Union foreign policy chief Javier Solana also congratulated Serbian President Boris Tadic and the Serbian government. Solana said the arrest demonstrated Belgrade’s willingness to cooperate with the U.N. tribunal and could help advance Serbia’s bid for closer ties with the European Union.

Serbian officials portrayed the operation as evidence that the country’s new government was committed to fulfilling its international obligations.

Rasim Ljajic, the Serbian official responsible for cooperation with the Hague tribunal, said Karadzic had been detained in Serbia and that the legal process for his transfer had begun. War crimes prosecutor spokesman Bruno Vekaric said the arrest followed an operation by Serbian security services.

Karadzic’s attorney said he would challenge the transfer order, a move that could delay but was not expected to prevent his extradition.

Karadzic, a psychiatrist and poet before entering politics, became president of the self-declared Bosnian Serb republic during the Bosnian war. He disappeared from public view in 1996 after stepping down under international pressure.

His arrest leaves former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, also accused of genocide in connection with Srebrenica, among the tribunal’s most prominent remaining fugitives.

**BREAKING NEWS: Serbia Captures Radovan Karadžić, the Man Dubbed “Europe’s Osama bin Laden”**

**BELGRADE, Serbia —** Serbian authorities have arrested former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadžić, one of the world’s most wanted war-crimes suspects, ending a flight from justice that lasted nearly 13 years.

Karadžić, accused of genocide and crimes against humanity during Bosnia’s 1992–95 war, had been sought by the United Nations tribunal in The Hague over atrocities including the massacre of about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica and the prolonged siege of Sarajevo.

His capture is comparable in symbolic terms to catching “Europe’s Osama bin Laden”: the arrest of a fugitive whose name became synonymous with mass killing and who evaded an international manhunt for years. The analogy reflects his notoriety rather than any operational connection to al-Qaeda.

Serbian officials said Karadžić had been living in Belgrade under a false identity, reportedly practicing alternative medicine and disguising himself with a long beard and glasses. He is expected to be transferred to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia to face trial.

The arrest is also a major political turning point for Serbia. The European Union has repeatedly made closer ties—and ultimately EU membership—dependent on Belgrade’s full cooperation with the war-crimes tribunal. Karadžić’s detention provides powerful evidence that Serbia’s new, pro-European government is prepared to confront fugitives long protected or tolerated by nationalist networks.

EU officials are likely to view the move as an important step toward unblocking deeper economic and political integration. But the case will not completely remove the issue from Serbia’s path: former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladić, also charged over Srebrenica and Sarajevo, remains at large.

Karadžić’s arrest therefore carries significance on two fronts. For survivors of the Bosnian war, it offers the prospect of long-delayed accountability. For Serbia, it signals a choice to move away from the nationalist legacy of the 1990s and toward membership in the European mainstream.

## Radovan Karadžić arrested in Belgrade

**BELGRADE, July 2008** — Serbian authorities arrested former Bosnian Serb political leader **Radovan Karadžić** on 21 July 2008 after nearly 13 years as one of the world’s most wanted war-crimes fugitives. He had been living in Belgrade under the false identity **Dragan Dabić**, presenting himself as a practitioner of alternative medicine.

Karadžić was transferred to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague. At the time of his arrest, he faced charges including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the 1992–95 Bosnian war.

### Sarajevo and Srebrenica allegations

Prosecutors alleged that, as president of the self-proclaimed Bosnian Serb republic and its supreme commander, Karadžić was a central figure in campaigns to remove Bosnian Muslims and Croats from Serb-claimed territory.

The charges included responsibility for the **siege of Sarajevo**, during which Bosnian Serb forces subjected the city to prolonged shelling and sniper fire. The siege lasted from 1992 to 1995 and killed thousands of civilians.

Karadžić was also accused of responsibility for the **July 1995 Srebrenica massacre**, in which Bosnian Serb forces killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys after capturing the UN-declared “safe area.” International courts have classified the killings as genocide.

Karadžić denied criminal responsibility. He was later convicted by the ICTY in 2016; on appeal in 2019, his sentence was increased from 40 years to life imprisonment.

### Praise for the arrest

The arrest was widely welcomed by:

- **Bosnian victims’ and survivors’ groups**, which described it as an overdue step toward justice.
- **The United Nations, European Union and United States**, which praised Serbia’s cooperation with international justice.
- **Western governments and Serbian pro-European leaders**, who said the action demonstrated a break with the nationalist policies associated with the wars of the 1990s.
- Supporters of Serbia’s EU membership, who viewed the arrest as removing a major obstacle to closer European integration.

### Criticism and controversy

The arrest also prompted criticism:

- **Serbian nationalist parties and Karadžić supporters** portrayed him as a wartime defender of the Serb people and condemned his transfer to The Hague. Demonstrations in Belgrade led to clashes with police.
- Some critics accused the Serbian government of acting primarily to gain political and economic benefits from the European Union.
- Members of Karadžić’s family and legal team questioned the official account of when and how he was detained and complained about delays in access to counsel.
- Some survivors, while welcoming the arrest, criticized Serbian authorities and the international community for allowing him to remain free for so long and stressed that an arrest could not by itself provide full justice or reconciliation.

The detention was nevertheless regarded internationally as a major development in efforts to hold senior political and military leaders accountable for atrocities committed during the breakup of Yugoslavia.

# Serbia Captures Bosnian Serb Wartime Leader Radovan Karadzic

**BELGRADE, July 22, 2008** — Serbian authorities have arrested Radovan Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb political leader accused of genocide and crimes against humanity during the 1992-95 Bosnian war, ending one of Europe’s most prominent war-crimes manhunts after nearly 13 years.

President Boris Tadic’s office announced late Monday that Karadzic had been located and detained by Serbia’s security services. The government said he had been brought before an investigative judge in Belgrade and that proceedings had begun for his transfer to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, or ICTY, in The Hague.

“Radovan Karadzic was located and arrested,” Tadic’s office said in a brief statement. The arrest, carried out only days after a new Serbian government took office, was widely seen as evidence that Belgrade intended to strengthen cooperation with the tribunal and accelerate Serbia’s efforts to join the European Union.

Karadzic, 63, had been living in Belgrade under the assumed identity **Dragan Dabic**, according to Serbian officials. Photographs released after his arrest showed him with a long white beard, glasses and hair tied back, a striking departure from his wartime appearance. Officials said he had worked openly as a practitioner of alternative medicine and had moved around the capital without attracting public attention.

Rasim Ljajic, the Serbian official responsible for cooperation with the Hague tribunal, said Karadzic’s false identity was “very convincing” and that he had been earning money through alternative medical work. Vladimir Vukcevic, Serbia’s war-crimes prosecutor, said the fugitive had been arrested in Belgrade after surveillance by the security services.

Karadzic’s lawyer, Sveta Vujacic, disputed aspects of the official account, saying his client had been detained several days before the government announced the arrest. Serbian authorities rejected that version.

## Accused of genocide and the siege of Sarajevo

Karadzic was the wartime president of the self-declared Bosnian Serb republic and the supreme political leader of forces commanded by General Ratko Mladic. Prosecutors at the ICTY alleged that the two men were central participants in a campaign to remove Bosnian Muslims and Croats from territory claimed by Bosnian Serbs.

The tribunal’s indictment charged Karadzic with **genocide, complicity in genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war**. The allegations focused on several major elements of the Bosnian conflict:

- **The Srebrenica massacre:** Prosecutors accused Karadzic of responsibility for the July 1995 killing of more than 7,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys after Bosnian Serb forces seized the United Nations-declared “safe area” of Srebrenica. International courts have classified the massacre as genocide.
- **The siege of Sarajevo:** He was charged over a campaign of shelling and sniper fire directed at civilians in the Bosnian capital. The siege lasted nearly four years and killed thousands of people.
- **Ethnic persecution across Bosnia:** The indictment alleged that Bosnian Serb forces carried out killings, expulsions, unlawful detention, torture and the destruction of homes and religious buildings as part of an effort to permanently remove non-Serbs from targeted areas.
- **The taking of U.N. hostages:** Karadzic was also accused of responsibility for the seizure of United Nations peacekeepers in 1995, some of whom were chained to potential NATO targets in an attempt to prevent airstrikes.

The charges were allegations to be tested at trial. Karadzic had repeatedly rejected the tribunal’s authority and denied responsibility for atrocities committed during the war.

## Western governments welcome arrest

The capture drew immediate praise from European and American officials, many of whom had long argued that Serbia’s failure to arrest Karadzic and Mladic obstructed reconciliation in the Balkans.

European Union foreign-policy chief **Javier Solana** called the arrest “very good news” and said it demonstrated the determination of Serbia’s new government to cooperate with international justice.

European Commission President **José Manuel Barroso** described the detention as “a very important step forward for Serbia’s European aspirations.” EU officials had made full cooperation with the Hague tribunal a central condition for closer relations with Belgrade.

British Foreign Secretary **David Miliband** said Karadzic’s capture showed that “there can be no hiding place for those who are indicted for war crimes.” He said the arrest was important for the victims of the Bosnian conflict and for Serbia’s future in Europe.

Former U.S. diplomat **Richard Holbrooke**, the chief architect of the 1995 Dayton peace agreement that ended the Bosnian war, welcomed the arrest of a man he had once described as “the Osama bin Laden of Europe.” Holbrooke said Karadzic had been one of the principal figures responsible for the bloodshed in Bosnia and called his detention a major victory for justice.

The White House also welcomed the development. U.S. officials said the arrest honored the victims of the war and would help Serbia move toward greater integration with European and transatlantic institutions.

At the United Nations, Secretary-General **Ban Ki-moon** said the arrest marked “a historic moment for the victims” of the crimes alleged against Karadzic.

## Political impact inside Serbia

The arrest exposed Serbia’s continuing divisions over the wars that accompanied the breakup of Yugoslavia.

Tadic and the pro-European coalition government presented cooperation with the tribunal as both a legal obligation and a necessary step toward EU membership. Foreign Minister **Vuk Jeremic** said the arrest showed that Serbia was serious about upholding international law and fulfilling its commitments.

Former prime minister **Vojislav Kostunica**, a nationalist critic of the Hague tribunal, condemned the new government’s approach. His Democratic Party of Serbia argued that the arrest harmed national interests and accused the authorities of placing Western demands above the treatment of Serbs accused by the tribunal.

Tomislav Nikolic, then a leading figure in the nationalist Serbian Radical Party, also criticized the detention. Nationalist groups announced demonstrations in Belgrade, and police increased security around government buildings and foreign embassies.

The arrest nevertheless represented a significant change in Serbia’s political direction. Karadzic had remained at large through several governments, prompting repeated accusations that he was protected by nationalist networks and elements within the security establishment.

## Years in hiding

Karadzic was indicted by the ICTY in 1995 but disappeared from public view after the Bosnian war. For years, international forces searched monasteries, mountain villages and suspected safe houses in Bosnia, Serbia and Montenegro.

His ability to establish a new life in the Serbian capital surprised investigators. Under the Dabic identity, he reportedly lectured on alternative health, contributed to a medical magazine and maintained a website advertising treatments for sexual and psychological conditions.

Officials said the disguise and false documents allowed him to live without relying on the conspicuous armed protection networks that had helped shield some wartime suspects in the years immediately after the conflict.

Karadzic’s relatives and supporters had long maintained that the United States had promised him immunity if he withdrew from public life after the Dayton agreement. Holbrooke repeatedly denied making such a deal, and the ICTY said any alleged promise would not invalidate its indictment.

## Transfer to The Hague

Under Serbian law, Karadzic was entitled to challenge his transfer. Once the legal process was completed, he was expected to be flown to the Netherlands and placed in the tribunal’s detention unit at Scheveningen, near The Hague.

His arrest left Mladic as the most prominent Bosnian Serb fugitive still sought by the tribunal. Former Croatian Serb leader Goran Hadzic also remained at large.

For survivors of Srebrenica and Sarajevo, Karadzic’s detention carried exceptional symbolic weight. More than a decade after the conflict ended, the former Bosnian Serb leader—once among the most powerful men in the Balkans—was finally set to face judges on charges arising from Europe’s deadliest war since the Second World War.
